overview: This file traces U.S. reporting and planning concerning Japanese-ruled Taiwan (Formosa) from 1940 to 1944. It begins with diplomatic intelligence about a reportedly violent farmers’ revolt and Japanese plans to use Taiwan’s colonial-development experience in Hainan, then documents State Department concern over duplicative wartime research by several U.S. agencies. Later papers address prospective Allied military government and financial administration after occupation, while the final despatch and enclosure provide detailed—though sometimes uncertain or numerically inconsistent—intelligence on Taiwan’s economy, population, military conditions, anti-Japanese underground parties, propaganda opportunities, and possible postwar status.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Grew reporting a farmers’ revolt in Taiwan
subfiles.about: Reports an alleged August 1940 revolt by Taiwanese Chinese farmers against Japanese agricultural controls.
subfiles.summary: A source described as reliable reported that farmers revolted in several Taiwanese villages around August 20 and killed more than one hundred Japanese. The unrest was attributed to low fixed rice prices and restrictions on cultivating the more profitable sugar crop; Japanese authorities allegedly suppressed it mercilessly with heavy loss of life.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Hoshino’s plans for Taiwan and Hainan
subfiles.about: Relays Naoki Hoshino’s public argument that Taiwan’s accumulated colonial expertise should support Japan’s southward expansion and the development of Hainan.
subfiles.summary: Hoshino declared that Taiwan’s industrial development had reached its limit because of scarce land but that its expertise could be redirected toward Japan’s southward policy. He presented Hainan as a promising military base and field for Japanese agricultural, mineral, and economic activity, stressing its supposed similarities to Taiwan and Japan. Development of the island was also portrayed as a demonstration to foreign countries of Japanese capacity to settle and work efficiently in tropical climates.

subfiles.title: Adviser’s memorandum on coordinating Taiwan research
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.about: Suggests ways for the State Department to reduce duplication among agencies researching Taiwan and the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Responding to the February 14 memorandum, the adviser proposes preparing a comprehensive departmental study for circulation among interested agencies. Other possibilities include consulting Commerce and Navy materials, surveying secondary literature through the National Geographic Society and Library of Congress, or asking the agencies to pool their inquiries and conduct a joint study.

subfiles.title: Routing note asking how to handle the Taiwan research problem
subfiles.to: Office of the Adviser on Political Relations; Mr. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Asks whether the proposed method is the best way to handle the interagency research question.
subfiles.summary: The brief handwritten or typed routing note asks the Office of the Adviser on Political Relations whether the matter is being handled in the best way. A departmental stamp records its receipt by Mr. Hornbeck on February 17, 1942.

subfiles.title: Covering memorandum distributing the Far Eastern Affairs study
subfiles.to: Mr. McDermott; Mr. Wilson; Mr. Ballantine
subfiles.about: Transmits an attached memorandum concerning the preparation of government reports about the Far East.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs circulates its memorandum on problems arising in the preparation of Far Eastern reports. The three recipients are invited, at their discretion, to supply copies to the offices with which they are associated.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on duplicated U.S. Government research concerning Taiwan
subfiles.to: State Department officials and liaison officers
subfiles.about: Describes overlapping requests from U.S. military, economic-warfare, and information agencies for reports and expert assistance concerning Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Military Intelligence, the Office of the Coordinator of Information, and the Board of Economic Warfare were separately preparing overlapping studies of Taiwan and repeatedly requesting consular reports or interviews with State Department specialists. The memorandum notes practical problems in copying lengthy original reports and suggests that agencies coordinate oral inquiries to avoid duplicated effort. A comparable failure of internal communication is illustrated by a propaganda inquiry about Thailand whose requester did not know of either an existing State Department memorandum or Kenneth Landon’s expertise.

subfiles.title: Report of meeting on financial directives for Japan and Taiwan
subfiles.from: Division of Financial and Monetary Affairs
subfiles.about: Records interdepartmental discussion of financial directives for prospective military governments in Japan and Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Representatives of the War, Navy, Treasury, and State Departments reviewed draft financial directives for Japan and Taiwan. Lieutenant Commander Gluckstadt argued that Taiwan would require much more direct and detailed Allied administration because Japanese personnel controlled government and industry, while the overwhelmingly Chinese population was expected to reject Japanese authority and possibly attack Japanese residents. Participants accepted the distinction provisionally and postponed detailed consideration of the Taiwan directive.

subfiles.title: Gauss despatch forwarding a report on political conditions in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, U.S. Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.about: Forwards an Office of War Information report based on an interview with Formosa Investigation Committee member Hsieh Nan-kuang.
subfiles.summary: Gauss refers to an earlier despatch about the formation of the Formosa Problems Investigation Committee. He encloses a report entitled “Political Conditions in Formosa,” prepared by an Office of War Information officer from an interview with Hsieh Nan-kuang, a Chinese Military Affairs Commission official and committee member.

subfiles.title: Political Conditions in Formosa
subfiles.from: Theodore Herman, China Division, Office of War Information
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy and interested U.S. agencies
subfiles.about: Summarizes Hsieh Nan-kuang’s account of Taiwan’s economy, population, military conditions, underground politics, and suitability for Allied propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Hsieh described strategic industries around Takao, agricultural extraction for Japan, troop-training areas, labor conscription, military service, and the social hardship allegedly imposed on Taiwanese families. He outlined the island’s Chinese, Japanese, and Indigenous populations and identified three anti-Japanese underground movements: the Kuomintang, the Communist Party, and the Revolutionary Peoples’ League, whose postwar programs ranged from union with China to dominion status or independence. He also recommended bilingual broadcasting and leaflets, bomb warnings, war news, encouragement of underground activity, and appeals concerning the treatment and return of Taiwanese servicemen. Several population and party-activity figures appear internally inconsistent or were marked as uncertain by the report’s compiler.

interest: The file is valuable because it brings together several distinct layers of wartime knowledge production: diplomatic rumor, Japanese imperial rhetoric, bureaucratic debate over intelligence coordination, occupation planning, and information obtained from a politically connected Taiwanese exile. It documents how U.S. planners came to view Taiwan as administratively different from Japan because colonial institutions were dominated by Japanese personnel while most inhabitants were Chinese. The final report is especially useful for studying competing visions of Taiwan’s future—incorporation into China, dominion status, or independence—and the construction of Allied psychological-warfare policy, although its striking statistics and claims about underground membership require careful corroboration.
